references.text: The official had already asked Jesus to come down and heal his son, and Jesus pointed out that people do not believe unless they see signs and wonders. Verse 49 shows that the father's desperation outweighs Jesus' rebuke – he repeats his plea even more urgently ([ref:Joh 4:47-48|John 4:47-48]).

Jesus heals from a distance with only His word, without going down to Capernaum. The official's faith grows from demanding Jesus' physical presence (v. 49) to believing in Jesus' word alone ([ref:Joh 4:50-53|John 4:50-53]).

Jairus begs Jesus urgently to come and lay hands on his daughter, who is at the point of death. A parallel situation where a father asks Jesus to come before the child dies ([ref:Mark 5:23|Mark 5:23]).

The officer in Capernaum also asks Jesus for healing, but unlike the official in John 4, he specifically asks Jesus only to say a word. Both accounts demonstrate Jesus' power to heal from a distance ([ref:Matt 8:5-8|Matthew 8:5-8]).
Martha says to Jesus: "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died." The same idea that Jesus' physical presence is necessary for Him to be able to help ([ref:Joh 11:21|John 11:21]).

Mary also falls at Jesus' feet and expresses the same as Martha – that if He had been there, her brother would not have died. The same reasoning as the official: Jesus' physical presence is seen as a prerequisite for help ([ref:Joh 11:32|John 11:32]).

Naaman expected the prophet Elisha to come out personally and perform specific actions to heal him. A parallel to the official's belief that Jesus had to come down physically in order for healing to occur ([ref:2 Kong 5:11|2 Kings 5:11]).

At the wedding in Cana, Jesus seemingly refused His mother's request, yet acted anyway. A similar pattern in John 4:48-50: Jesus appears to reject the official's plea, but responds with healing ([ref:Joh 2:4|John 2:4]).
